technical-data.invention-title: METHOD FOR MANUFACTURING TRANSPARENT MEMBERS, SUCH AS GLASS AND THE LIKE, AND ARTICLES OBTAINED WITH THE METHOD ITSELF
PROCEDE DE FABRICATION DE SUBSTANCES TRANSPARENTES, TELLES QUE DU VERRE OU ANALOGUE, ET ARTICLES AINSI OBTENUS

abstract.p: Method for manufacturing transparent members (10) consisting in forming a chamber (11) between two plates (14, 16), by interposing gaskets and/or rigid profiles (12, 18) and sealing the chamber (11) to maintain the liquid therein. It is possible that one of the plates (14, 16), defining the chamber (11), is provided with valve means to allow admission, removal and replacement of the liquid, or the same valve means is located on the perimeter of the chamber (11).

Cette invention concerne un procédé de fabrication de substances transparentes (10) consistant à former une chambre (11) entre deux plaques (14, 16) au moyen de joints intercalaires et/ou de profilés rigides (12, 18) et à rendre cette chambre étanche pour empêcher le liquide qu'elle contient de fuir. L'une des plaques (14, 16) qui définissent la chambre (11) peut être assortie d'un dispositif réglant l'admission, l'évacuation et le remplacement du liquide. Ce dispositif peut également être monté à la périphérie de la chambre (11).

description.p: METHOD FOR MANUFACTURING TRANSPARENT MEMBERS, SUCH AS GLASS AND THE LIKE, AND ARTICLES OBTAINED WITH THE METHOD ITSELF
Present invention refers to a method for manufacturing transparent members of glass, or the like, to be used as decorative and pictorial coatings for posters, buildings and furniture.

Specifically, present invention refers to a method for giving particular desired colours to transparent or semitransparent members of glass, or the like, however avoiding to apply solid and irremovable dyes to said members making possible to change colours without difficult and expensive operations, such as peeling, cleaning and new painting of the members to which it is willing to change colour.

Also more specifically, present invention intends to give desired and variable colours to large size vertically arranged surfaces, such as coating panels of rooms, building fronts, doors, windows and the like.

Presently, vitreous and plastic transparent materials are coloured with specific paints, usually surface smeared either on one of two opposed faces, in order to let appear the colour through the thickness of the member, or on both faces of the member, loosing however the depth sensation given by the transparency.

A surface smeared paint is however prone to scratches, peeling and the like and it is very difficult, if not impossible to change its colour, if that were desired, owing to the strength of its adherence on smearing supports substantially preventing a removal thereof without undesired consequences.

Peeling of the paints, either through dissolving them by means of solvents, or through mechanical abrasion produce generally poor results because: a) many times a paint, once dried and chemically changed by setting process, is poorly soluble in solvents; b) unless the support is of glass, per se solvent insensitive, it happens that the solvent itself can etch and partially dissolve the support itself, as often occurs with many kinds of plastic supports;

c) the abrasives usually scratch the surfaces of the supports, which hardly can be polished to make them transparent enough.
Generally the above mentioned paint removing systems appeared difficult and labour consuming, being so expensive, to make often less expensive to replace an article than to however rework it.

As a first attempt to overcome the above mentioned drawbacks and make easily painted substantially transparent supports, it has been devised to paint the inside of an article, by completely insulating of the colour from external agents and then saving transparency, brightness and hue variant. Such an attempt has some success, however maintains the drawback of the impossibility of however changing both the colours and the images formed inside the article.

As a second attempt, it has been devised to make a transparent pane, provided with at least a chamber comprised between at least two transparent plates, to be filled with a coloured liquid, to change on will the colour of the pane, by changing the liquid admitted in the chamber.
The prior art lists a number of chambers, according to this attempt, comprised between transparent panes to be filled with either moving or steady coloured liquids.

For example, US- A-3, 706,249 discloses a display device, for producing colour effects, consisting of at least two separated liquid sealed chambers defined between at least three optically transparent plates, containing at least two differently coloured liquids, in which are admitted from the bottom air bubbles which, climbing into the chambers produce random variable chromatic effects. Such a device produces just an aesthetic effect due to the bubbles climbing and floating along the chamber.

US-A-3,898,781 discloses a structure of a transparent floor tile comprising a chamber, defined between two transparent face plates, to be filled with a viscous liquid mixed with air bubbles and, possibly, solid bodies thinner in thickness than the chamber and different in colour from the viscous liquid. At least one of the face plates is flexible enough to allow under the operation of an external force, such as the weight of people walking on the floor tile, the movement of the
bubbles and of the solid bodies and the possible fraction of the bubbles in smaller bubbles with apparent variable aesthetic effects. Such a system produces the said aesthetic effects, which appear variable, but poorly controllable, and further it is just suited for horizontally arranged articles, such as floor tiles, because, having at least a compliant face, it is not suitable to a chamber to be vertically arranged which would be distorted under the weight of the liquid. Thus the system is not suited to large size plates to be vertically installed.

US-A-4,034,493 discloses a movable display device, to be arranged according to two each other reversed orientations comprised of two either transparent or translucent plates, defining between them a closed chamber, provided at the top and the bottom with two respective reservoirs, containing one of the reservoirs a first liquid and the other reservoir with the chamber containing a second liquid, being the two liquids each other immixible, different enough in density and one, for example the first one, heavier than the other. When the device is arranged with the reservoir of the heavier liquid on the top, the liquid itself flows down through the closed chamber separating itself in liquid drops or beads which, by flowing along obstacles arranged in the chamber, produce aesthetic effects substantially random changing. At last, the heavier liquid is collected in the lower reservoir from which it can come out, to repeat the aesthetic effect just by reversing the orientation of the device, so that the bottom side becomes the top side, allowing a reverse migration of the heavier liquid and repeating the same random aesthetic effects. Such a device produces some aesthetic effects, but having to be reversed for continuing the aesthetic effects, may have just limited size and thus it is not suited to embody tall vertical chambers having the size of the walls of a room.

US-A-4,057,493 discloses a decorative device comprising two chambers, defined between three transparent plates, each containing two immixible liquids having different densities and colours such as to have different chromatic effects which can random change when the orientation of the device is reversed to have the former upper side becoming the lower side. Also this device, as the device disclosed in US-A-4,034,493, is not suited to embody tall vertical chambers.
US-A-4,085,533 discloses a device for producing aesthetic effects within closed containers by inputting therein at least three liquids different in density and each other immixible, arranging the three liquids one on top of the other according to their decreasing density. Means for moving at least one of the liquids, such as pumps, for producing aesthetic effects movable inside the containers themselves. Also such a device is useful for producing aesthetic effects, also movable, in a more or less random way, however just in limited size containers, as in its disclosure nothing is told about the shape, the size and the orientation of the containers and no provisions are taken for enhancing the strength of the walls and the bottom of large size chambers.

US-A-4,395,835 discloses a device providing in two chambers, defined by three adjacent transparent plates, different effects of layered colours, when the device is standing, and colours multiple, strongly variable in a complex and random way when the device is distorted and reversed. Such a device, having to be movable, can have just limited size and its disclosure reveals nothing useful for the solution of the technical problems faced by the present invention.

All the above listed prior art publications give for granted the solution of the problems of how to seal the chambers to be filled with coloured liquids, how to assure a sufficient adhesion between plates forming the chambers, how to resist the pressure of the liquids tending to move apart the plates and how to avoid that the coloured liquids filling the chambers can etch the sealing of the chambers or the adhesive joining the plates themselves. Unfortunately the above problems are still existing and one of the duties of the present invention is to solve them.

The above mentioned problems are overcome by the present invention providing a method for manufacturing transparent members, obtained by forming inside an article to be coloured chambers suited to be filled by one or more coloured liquids, characterized in that the chambers are embodied inside plate assemblies, of which at least one of them is transparent, by overlapping at least two of the plates and inserting a gasket peripherally arranged for defining the chambers.
Particularly, the two plates are surrounded by a containing profile pressing the gasket.
Alternatively, the two plates are tied by adhesives arranged outside the gasket.
Particularly, the two plates are each other parallel and are made of materials showing substantially equal physical features.
In addition, one of the plates is treated with reflecting materials, such as paints or silver coatings.
Also, to one of the plates is coupled a plate of metal or other reflecting material.

Moreover, a coloured liquid, such as water, a glycol, hydrocarbons and the like, allowing transparency and colouring, is admitted into the chambers through at least one hole provided with sealing means allowing admittance and replacement of the liquid itself.
Preferably the holes are more than one in number. Particularly, the liquid admittance occurs through a hole in a platelet arranged on a surface of one of the two wall plates.
Alternatively, the admission of the liquid occurs from holes pierced in the containing perimeter structural bar.
Further alternatively, on the wall plates defining the chamber, are made grindings in which the admittance plate and hole are inserted.
Preferably, the walls are ground along their perimeter for obtaining a slot to be filled by sealing means.
Particularly, the containing profile spans two grindings lowering the thickness of the two wall plates defining the camber with the sealing gasket.
Alternatively, instead of lowering the height of the plates by grinding them, two safety plates are joined to the plates defining the chamber with the sealing gasket.

Particularly, the wall plates are ground for containing a metal profile having cross-section size larger than the desired thickness of the camber.
According to a particular embodiment, the method forms an assembly of wall plates having, in front of the chamber to be filled with liquid, a transparent or semitransparent image, provided by a film sandwiched between two transparent plates.
Preferably, this embodiment with incorporated image can be transparent or semitransparent to be back illuminated.
Alternatively, this embodiment with incorporated image can be provided with reflecting bottom to be front illuminated.

The method, according to the invention, is characterized by admitting a coloured liquid, such as an alcohol, a glycol, a hydrocarbon or similar liquids, allowing sufficient transparency and intensive enough colouring, through a hole properly located for a distribution thereof in desired portions and provided with sealing means allowing both admission and removal of the liquid itself.
Preferably, glass plates, or similar transparent plates, among which cavities or chambers shaped according to desired drawings are formed, are each other joined by means of adhesive or resin films.
Particularly preferably, the plates can be joined along their external perimeter and the each other faced chambers, defined between two plates, are filled with one of the coloured liquids.

According to an alternative embodiment, it is possible to "inflate" an interface between planar plates with a pressurised coloured liquid to form a lenticular shape able to produce variable colours and hues due to the thickness of the injected liquid.

According to another alternative embodiment, some plates can be coupled with adhesives both along the perimeter and on portions of the internal depiction field of images, so forming a "sandwich" provided with one or more internal chambers.

In particular, the coupling is obtained with a film of plastic material used in the production of safety glass plates, being the thickness of the film used for defining the chambers to be filled with the coloured liquid, resulting the thickness of the chambers equal to that of the film.
Preferably, the thickness of the film ranges between a few tenths of millimetre and a few millimetres.

Further preferably, to embody a drawing appearing between the plates, the film is cut out in advance according to the desired drawing, by removing the portions intended to provide the chamber to be filled with liquid.
Preferably, these lacking portions form large chambers for producing uniform colour panes.
In a first alternative, the lacking portions are small inlays for ornamental purposes, such as geometric drawings, floreal motives or the like.
In a second alternative, they can depict technical drawings representing maps and/or operations of plants and/or industrial processes.
In a third alternative, the inlays can depict scientific and didactical representations, such as animal and vegetal circulatory systems.

In addition, can be devised combinations of more superimposed chambers obtained by coupling many glass plates, or the like, possibly, each other communicating through holes in the thickness of the interposed plates, which make possible the creation of many colour drawings by admission of different coloured liquids driven to different chambers.
Also, in the case of many level chambers, devices, providing the liquid distribution, can be hidden by properly arranged painting, and either mirror or half-mirror metal coatings.

According to another embodiment, it is possible to think to circulate two immixible liquids, by admitting them from coaxial ducts and removing them from different ducts arranged at different levels for having a threadlike flow of one of the liquids into one or more other liquids.

According to a further embodiment, it is possible to think to admit into a chamber defined between transparent plates two each other immixible liquids of very different density (as for example water and a hydrocarbon oil) to embody curtains having variable extension and transparency to be used as sun screens or anti-dazzle filters in automotive field.

In particular, the transparent plates defining at least a chamber can be so thin and/or flexible that an assembly thereof could be used as surface coating.
Preferably, the chambers can be sized in such a way to avoid or limit either yieldings or sackings due to the pressure connected to the head of the liquid in the chambers.
Alternatively, the chambers between the plates can be defined by using so- called "can" plates, that is already provided with chambers obtained, for example, by extrusion.

In the first embodiment, depicted in figure 1, it is seen how in a first pane 10 a chamber 11 is defined by a gasket 12 inserted, along the perimeter thereof, between two plates 14 and 16, for example glass plates. To the plates 14 and 16 is fastened a perimeter profilelδ, having resistant cross-section, pressing the gasket 12. Between the plates 14 and 16 and the profile 18 is interposed plastic and/or adhesive material 17 and 19.

A first advantage of such an embodiment is the perimeter protecting bar 18 avoiding chipping during subsequent movements. A second advantage consist in joining plates of different materials, for example glass with methacrylates or other plastic material, aluminium with glass, aluminium with methacrylates, etc. ...

An example is depicted in the second embodiment of figure 2 in which a second pane 20 comprises a chamber 21 defined by a first glass plate 24 and a second plate 26, for example of aluminium. Between the plates 24 and 26 is interposed a gasket 22, and the plates are retained by a perimeter profile28.

In a third embodiment, depicted in figure 3, it is provided that in a third pane 30. provided with chamber 31 and plates 34 and 36, a chemically resistant gasket 32 is bonded by an external sealing adhesive 33. This adhesive 33 is applied by keeping the plates 34 and 36 and the interposed gasket 32 in compression till setting of the adhesive. Alternatively, can be used adhesives having shrink on drying.

In figure 4 is depicted a variant of the preceding assembly system of the third pane in which a set 40, with a chamber 41, bounded by a gasket 42, is defined by two glass plates 44 and 46 askew ground along the perimeter in order to assure a larger bonding surface and house a higher sealing matter mass 48.

To avoid any perimeter step, defined by the thickness of the perimeter structural bar, the plates can be ground at the thickness of the used structural bar. In figure 5 it is seen a set 50 of a fourth pane in which the two plates 54 and 56
have been ground along their perimeter, where the thickness of a chamber 51, so defined is determined by a gasket 52. Between the plates and the containing profile58 is interposed some sealing matter 57 and 59.

According to figure 6, is obtained a levelling between the plates and the external profile of a set 60 of a fifth pane, by using safety layered plates. Thus two plates 68 and 70, adjacent a chamber 61, are coupled by a film or resin 66 and 72 to external plates 64 and 74 of lesser size. Also in this case, a gasket 62 defines the thickness of the chamber 61. A containment perimeter profιle78 can be of plastic material or metal.

In the figures 7 and 8, it is seen that a sixth transparent pane 80 is formed by a first transparent plate 82, by a second transparent plate 84 and by an adhesive layer 86 in the form of a frame interposed between the plate 82 and the plate 84. When the two plates 82 and 84 are adjacent arranged and the adhesive layer 86 has been activated, between the two plates 82 and 84 a chamber 88 is formed having thickness of the same order of the adhesive layer 86, being such a chamber 88 to be filled with a liquid having the desired optical properties (for example, a liquid of desired colour). To help the admission of liquids in the chamber 88, can be used one or more grooves 90 dug at least along a side of, for example, the transparent plate 84. In addition, the groove 90 operates as an effective limit to the expansion of the adhesive layer 86, preventing it to spread beyond the groove inside the chamber 88. Preferably, the groove 90 is along the perimeter and adjacent the inside of the adhesive layer 86 shaped as a frame.

In figure 9 is depicted a seventh pane 100 formed by a first transparent plate 102 and by a second transparent plate 104 kept together by an adhesive layer 106, perimeter arranged as a frame, defining a chamber 108 between the plates 102 and 104. Such a pane allows, through admission of liquid under suitable pressure, easily determined by skilled people in this art, to inflate the chamber 108 in order to have a higher central thickness, sloping to the perimeter of the plates, to give the pane a substantially lenticular shape. Such a shape allows particular aesthetic effects when the chamber 108 is filled with coloured or not coloured liquids, having refraction index well different from the plates 102 and 104, if they were in
very thin layers, of the order of the wave length (λ) of the used light, because they could give the layers either shades or iridescence. Further, in the case that the pane were horizontally arranged, such as a plane of a table, the insertion of a gas bubble, such as air, would produce effects of variable images for any minimal strain due to weights laid on the table itself.

Let us consider the figures 10 and 11 depicting an eighth pane 110 particularly suited for the embodiment of plates having ornamental functions for pane of furniture, buildings and the like of the kind to be illuminated by reflection, having the purpose of coating opaque surfaces, Such a pane 110 comprises a first transparent plate 112 (for example glass) having downside a film 114, supporting for example xerographic images, resting on a sheet 116 of plastic material coupling two plates, such as polyvinyl butyral used for the layering of safety glasses. However, such a sheet 116 is not indispensable and can be omitted. Under the film 1 14, and the possible sheet 116, is arranged a translucent rather thick film 1 18, as, for example a glass etched by hydrofluoric acid vapours(HF) (acidified glass), having an inside translucent etching 119, to obtain light scattering effects. Between the translucent 118 and a below transparent plate 126 is inserted an adhesive layer 120, shaped as a perimeter frame, operating to connect the translucent plate 118 to the below transparent plate 126, leaving between them a chamber 122, filled by a liquid to be chosen for obtaining the desired aesthetic effects, being the chamber fed by a groove 124 for a uniform distribution of the coloured liquid. The transparent plate 126 (for example glass) rests on a coupling sheet 128 of the same material of the sheet 116, such as polyvinyl butyral, providing to connect the plate 126 to a mirror 130 comprising a plate provided with top grinding 131 and lower reflecting layer 132 (such as a silver coating) operating to reflect the light coming from the outside of the pane 110 without sharply reflect the external images, which could be undesirable. At last, a solid layer 134 protects the reflecting layer 132 to avoid accidental wear or peeling. Such a so complex assembly manages to produce changing reflecting surfaces in accordance to the colours of the liquids either admitted or circulated in the chamber 122 defined between plates 118 and 126. Also, by choosing to circulate a
pair of immixible liquids, of which one is moved as a threaded flow in the other one, particular aesthetic effects can be obtained.

Figure 12 depicts a ninth pane 140, which can be either transparent or reflecting, and is made of lenticular shape by pressurised liquid in a chamber internal in the same pane 140, as it occurs for the pane depicted in figure 9. Particularly, such a pane 140 is made of a first top plat 142, a bottom plate 144 and two intermediate plates 246 and 148, of which the plate 146 is translucent through treatment with hydrofluoric acid (HF) and the plate 148 illuminates by transparency or reflection the pane 140, being said plates 146 and 148 joined by an adhesive layer 150 arranged as a frame along the perimeters of the intermediate plates 146 and 148 each other faced. The liquid, used under pressure, gives a lenticular shape to a chamber 152 between the two plate sets, being the plates 142 and 146 deflected as they are more pliable than the below plates 148 and 144. An optional use of reflecting layers can make this pane suited for external illumination. While the omission of reflecting layers makes it suited to an internal illumination. The obtained effects are similar to that of the pane of figure 9.

To admit, take off, or replace coloured liquids, every chamber is provided with valve means or connecting systems. In figure 13 it is seen an assembly 160, consisting of two plates 164 and 166 delimiting a chamber 161, a gasket 162 retained by a profile 168 bonded by an adhesive 176. On the surface of one of the plates is pierced a hole and is inserted a plate 172 provided with a hole 174 having a thread and a abutment seat for a screw stopper.

In the case that plates of different materials are used, the plate 172 is fastened to the material easier to be worked and better to be sealed. In figure 14, for example, a pane 180 consists of a first glass plate 184, a gasket 182, a second plate 186 and a profile 188 defining together a chamber 181. The second plate 186 is of metallic material and a plate 190 is seam welded to the plate 186. It is self evident that such a plate 190 could better resist to possible tightening strains of a screw stopper 194 or other connecting systems.

In figurel 5 a pane 200 consists of a glass plate 204 which with a gasket 202, a profile 208 and a metal plate 206 defines a chamber 201. In such a case, a plate
210, having a support profile 211 inside the chamber 201, is inserted from inside and retained by an external nut 212 with a washer and a gasket.

In alternative to the above disclosed embodiments, it results easier to weld on the containing profile of the plates a nut and a relief in which could be pierced a threaded hole for admission of liquids and/or the fastening of the connecting or closing system. Such a solution avoids the piercing of the plates for connecting admission plates to the faces of one of these.

In figure 16 it is seen a tenth pane 220 comprised of two layered plates 224 and 226. To a containing profile 228 is fastened an admission plate 230 with admission hole 236 communicating with a chamber 221. A sealing ring 232 around the hole 236 assures a continuity with a gasket 234 interrupted at the hole 236.

The location of the hole(s) for admitting and/or replacing the liquids in the thickness of the pane has some advantages for the use, for example in glass members where this holes are internal with respect to traditional fastenings frames.

In figure 17 is depicted an eleventh pane provided with an interposed metallic profile. In such a pane 240 a metal profile 242 is bonded by adhesives 248 and 254 between two layered plates 244 and 246. these plates are ground on the internal face, or are of the here above mentioned "stepping" kind, and insdie used. The perimeter stepping of the plates allows to use profiles in which can be pierced necessary connecting holes 252 without raise the internal thickness of the chamber 241.

A variation is depicted in the figures 18 and 19, representing a pane 260 in which a metal profile 262 of reduced thickness, such as a strap 268, is interposed and bonded with glues, silicones, or the like, and its thickness defines a chamber 261. A hole 272, pierced in one of the glass plates, houses a nut 268, or the like, welded in advance to the profile 262. A hole or groove 265, in the thickness of the strap, connects the chamber 261 with a threaded hole 276 of the nut 268 and such a hole 276 end with an abutment seat for a screw stopper 278, which results
embedded. With such an approach it is possible to limit the protrusion of the closure and have a fastening of the admission plate surely pull and twist resistant.
The closure and/or connection fitting can be located on the pane thickness even if the external containing profile is not present.

Let us consider in the figures 20 and 21 a pane 280 assembled as in figure 3. A gasket 282 is tension tied by adhesives 302 while one or two admission plates 294 and 304 have a threaded hole 298 and 308 and are relief bonded on the thickness of plates 284 and 286 by means of an adhesive 292 assuring also the continuty of the seal given by the gasket 282.

In the preceding example the admission plates protrude from the outline of the plates, but for particular uses such a protrusion can be limited. In figure 22 a pane 310 is assembled as in figure 4. Plates 312 and 314 are further ground to obtain a seat for an admission plate 316 which is bonded by adhesives 318. In such a plate 316 is provided a hole 322, connecting a chamber 311 with the outside, and a screw stopper 324 for assuring the seal.

In the figures 23 and 24 is shown the fitting of a plate 338 embedded in the thickness of a pane 330. A chamber 331 is obtained, as in figure 3, by means a gasket 334 and an adhesive 336. Let us consider the pane 330. On a first plate 332 are placed the gasket 334, a layer of the adhesive 336 and the plate 338, substantially similar to an almond. For housing the plate 338 the first plate 332 and the second plate 346 are locally ground. The plate 338 has two lateral holes 348 and 352 for inserting heads of gaskets and a hole 342, for admitting liquids, complete with a stopper 344. A specific adhesive 354 bonds the plate 338 to the two plates 332 and 346 and assures seal continuity with the gasket 334.

Should be expected the admission of non aggressive liquids and should be used, instead of the gasket between the two plates some common silicones or other sealing matters, it would be useful some plate section, as depicted in figure 25. however allowing an easier insertion of sealing matter 362 between plates 364 and 366 defining a chamber 361 for a twelfth panel 360. Of course, it would result also easier to adopt the above mentioned admission systems, especially those not requiring plate drilling.

As it can be seen in figure 26, two plates 374 and 376 defining a chamber 371 of a thirteenth pane 370 are each other directly bonded by means of a sealing matter 372. A subsequent admission of liquids tends to bend the plates 374 and 376, producing a chamber 371 having cross-section slanting towards the perimeter. In case of admission of coloured liquids there will be shadowing effects on the colour. It results further interesting to use such a chamber for admitting liquid with different densities or an additional gas, causing the migration of the lighter fluids towards the centre of the chamber.

What has been here above disclosed refers some embodiments of the invention not to be absolutely held as limiting. Therefore, all those logical and equivalent changing which can be devised by a person skilled in this art, starting from the reading of the above disclosure, have to be considered within the scope of the invention as defined by the here below enclosed claims.
For example, instead of using two transparent planar plates, they could be used the so-called "can" plates, that is already provided with chamber obtained, for example, by extrusion.
